title: Sentence Rearrangement
summary: One PQRS jumble per Tier 1 shift and several paragraph jumbles in Tier 2 — all solved by the same chain method: tag each part's role (opener, pronoun continuation, contrast, conclusion), lock 2-3 mandatory pairs (noun→pronoun, a→the, cause→effect), then eliminate option strings layer by layer. Timeline markers and opener bans do most of the work.

subtopics.title: The PQRS method: label, anchor, chain, eliminate
subtopics.concept:
The classic item shows six labelled slots: sentence 1 fixed, sentence 6 fixed, and the four middle parts **P, Q, R, S** scrambled. The answer is a letter string (e.g. *QPSR*). Work it as a chain, not by trial:

1. **Read S1 and S6 first — they are free information.** S1 sets the topic; S6 shows where the thought must land.
2. **Read P, Q, R, S and tag each one's role:** opening of the middle (general statement), development (example/detail), contrast (but/however/now), conclusion (thus/so/that is why).
3. **Find the mandatory pairs** — a pronoun and its noun, a cause and its effect, a 'the' that needs an earlier 'a'. Pairs are unbreakable links.
4. **Chain the pairs and check the whole story** against S1 and S6.
5. **Eliminate option strings pair by pair:** each wrong string breaks some pair. If pair (S→must follow P) holds, only strings containing P-S survive; a second pair usually finishes the job. Never match four strings against the full story — kill them one broken link at a time.

**Role tags cheat-sheet:**

| Signal inside a part | Likely position |
|---|---|
| Full noun phrase, no pronouns, general statement | just after S1 |
| Pronoun (he, she, it, this, these) | right after the part naming its noun |
| But / However / Yet / Now | after the claim it contrasts |
| This has led to / As a result / Therefore | after the cause |
| Thus / Hence / That is why / The need of the hour | last, before S6 |
| One day / Last winter / Soon after | start of a time chain |

The method reduces a 4! = 24-case problem to about 3 comparisons — that is where its 30-second budget comes from.

tricks.title: Pairs before strings
tricks.body: Do not read the four option strings first. Build 2–3 mandatory pairs from P/Q/R/S; then check which strings respect them. Strings die by broken links, not by vibes.

tricks.title: S1–S6 frame test
tricks.body: After chaining, read S1 + your chain + S6 as one paragraph. If any 'it/this/they' lacks its noun, the chain is wrong.

tricks.title: Adjacent-swap distractors
tricks.body: Wrong strings usually swap two adjacent parts. Find the ONE swap each wrong string commits and name its broken pair — that is your verification.

mistakes: Reading all four strings against the full paragraph — slow and error-prone.
Letting a pronoun open the chain when its noun comes later.
Ignoring S6 — the conclusion word inside a middle part often belongs just before S6.
Forcing the string you 'like' instead of eliminating by pairs.
subtopics.notes:
### What the four middle parts are doing
Every PQRS middle is a small paragraph with a job to do between S1 and S6. Before you look at the options, give each part a one-word role:
- **Lead** — continues S1's subject with a general statement or a pronoun that points back to S1.
- **Support** — an example, a figure, a detail ('for example', 'in Kerala', 'children who read daily').
- **Turn** — a contrast or problem ('But', 'However', 'Yet', 'Sadly', 'Unfortunately').
- **Close** — a result, a solution or a lesson ('therefore', 'thus', 'that is why', 'the next step').
Once each part has a role, there are usually only one or two orders left to check.

### Two skeletons that cover most items
**Argument skeleton:** Lead -> Support -> Turn -> Close. *Solar power is spreading* -> panels light homes -> as a result children study -> however panels break down -> training technicians is therefore the next step.

**Problem skeleton:** Problem -> Cause -> Effect -> Response. *Lakes are dying* -> sewage flows in -> this fills them with weeds -> citizens now clean them. The Response part nearly always sits just before S6, because S6 usually looks ahead.

If the parts fit one skeleton, write the order down before you look at the options.

### S1 and S6 are clamps
- **S1 names the subject.** A part that begins 'Its route...', 'They do so because...' or 'The name referred to...' can only make sense directly after S1. That is the **S1 hook**, and it fixes the first letter.
- **S6 often points backwards.** 'It was the tastiest lunch...' needs the meal to have been mentioned just before; 'Subsidies for such machines...' needs the machines. Ask what S6's pronoun or 'such' points to. The part that supplies it is the last letter. That is the **S6 pull-back**.

With the first and last letters fixed, only two orders remain for the middle two parts, and one mandatory pair decides between them.

### The two-pair lock
Most items are designed so that two links settle everything. For example, with P-S (a pronoun pair) and R-Q (an 'as a result' pair), the answer must contain both blocks. Only PSRQ and RQPS are possible, and S1 or S6 decides which. Look for the two strongest links first instead of building the whole paragraph in your head.

### How setters build the wrong options
The three wrong strings are rarely random. Usually each one:
1. swaps two neighbouring parts (breaks one pair),
2. moves the Close part into the middle, or
3. opens with a pronoun or connector part.
When you pick your answer, name the link each wrong string breaks. If you cannot find one, check again.

### Quick revision
- Tag every part: Lead, Support, Turn, Close.
- Argument: Lead -> Support -> Turn -> Close. Problem: Problem -> Cause -> Effect -> Response.
- S1 hook fixes the first part; S6 pull-back fixes the last one.
- Two strong pairs usually decide the item — find them before reading the options.
- Every wrong string breaks a pair: name the pair it breaks.

patterns.name: Argument skeleton (claim, support, turn, close)
patterns.howToSpot: S1 makes a general claim; one part adds a detail or result, one begins with However/Yet, one carries therefore/thus.
patterns.logic:
1. Tag the parts: Lead, Support, Turn, Close.
2. Place the Support directly after what it supports (look for 'as a result', 'for this reason').
3. The Turn follows the good news it contradicts; the Close sits before S6.

*Why it works:* opinion paragraphs in exams almost always follow this fixed order.

example.q: S1: Solar power is spreading. Parts: panels light homes / as a result children study / however these panels break down / training technicians is therefore the next step.
example.solution: Lead (panels) -> Support ('as a result') -> Turn ('However, these panels') -> Close ('therefore') before S6.

patterns.name: Problem skeleton (problem, cause, effect, response)
patterns.howToSpot: S1 states a problem (lakes dying, stubble burning); parts give a reason, a consequence introduced by 'This has...', and a response or remedy.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the cause part — it explains S1 directly ('Untreated sewage flows in', 'They do so because').
2. Attach the effect to it ('This has filled...').
3. The response or remedy goes last, just before S6.

*Why it works:* a remedy cannot come before the harm it answers, so the chain runs in only one direction.

example.q: S1: Lakes are dying. Parts: sewage flows in / this has filled them with weeds / as the weeds choke the water, fish vanish / citizens now clean them.
example.solution: Cause -> 'This has' effect -> 'the weeds' result -> response last.

patterns.name: S6 pull-back
patterns.howToSpot: S6 begins with a pronoun, 'such', or a word that needs something mentioned just before it (It was the tastiest lunch; Subsidies for such machines).
patterns.logic:
1. Read S6 first and circle what it points back to.
2. The part that supplies that noun is the last part.
3. Build the rest backwards from it.

*Why it works:* S6 is fixed, so whatever it refers to must come directly before it.

example.q: S6: It was the tastiest lunch the school had ever served. One part: The harvest was cooked for the midday meal.
example.solution: 'It' in S6 = the midday meal, so the harvest part is last; the other three follow the growing season before it.

patterns.name: S1 hook
patterns.howToSpot: One part begins with a word that only makes sense directly after S1: Its route..., The name referred to..., They do so because...
patterns.logic:
1. Find the part whose first words point to S1's subject or action.
2. Make it the first letter.
3. Continue the chain from it using pairs.

*Why it works:* 'The name' or 'They do so' has nothing to refer to anywhere except S1.

example.q: S1: Chess was born in India as a game called chaturanga. Part: The name referred to the four divisions of an ancient army.
example.solution: 'The name' = chaturanga in S1, so this part comes first; 'These divisions' must follow it.

patterns.name: Two-pair lock
patterns.howToSpot: Two parts are tied by pronouns or 'this + noun', and another two by 'as a result', 'because of these', or 'Its price'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the two strongest pairs and write them as blocks.
2. Only two strings can contain both blocks.
3. Use S1 or S6 to choose between them.

*Why it works:* two unbreakable blocks cut 24 possible orders down to two.

example.q: Parts: He used sand and clay / Because of these cheap materials, it cost little / Its low price made it popular / Impressed by this demand, an agency ordered more.
example.solution: Each part points back to the one before it, so the chain is fixed: materials -> cost -> price -> demand.

subtopics.title: Opening and closing sentence clues
subtopics.concept:
**What cannot open** (the fast eliminations):
- A **bare pronoun** — 'He refused the offer' cannot start; nobody knows who 'he' is.
- A **conjunction or connector** — But, However, Therefore, So, And, Because cannot open a passage's thought.
- A **'the' on a first mention** — 'The boy ran' cannot open; a 'boy' must exist first.
- A **consequence phrase** — 'This decision proved costly' cannot open; there is no decision yet.

**What can open:** a full noun phrase with a general or scene-setting statement, a time-frame opener (One day, Last winter, In those days), or a definition.

**What closes well:**
- A **result or summary** — Therefore, Thus, Hence, That is why, The need of the hour.
- A **judgement or lesson** — moral-of-the-story sentences.
- A **future glance** — 'Life returned to normal after a week', 'Such campaigns must continue.'

**The cloze-style check:** S1 gives the subject; the first middle part usually continues that subject with a pronoun or elaboration. If two parts both look openable, prefer the more general one — specific examples come after general claims.

| Clue | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 'It improves memory.' as candidate opener | No — 'It' hangs |
| 'Reading improves memory.' as candidate opener | Yes — full noun, general |
| 'But books are costly.' | No — 'But' cannot open |
| 'Thus a reading habit pays for life.' | No — conclusion word |
| 'That is why libraries matter.' | Close only — final position |

tricks.title: Pronoun-orphan test
tricks.body: Any part starting with he/she/it/they/this/these needs its noun earlier. If no earlier part in a string supplies the noun, that string dies.

tricks.title: Connector ban
tricks.body: But/However/Therefore/Thus/So cannot open. Two of four options often open with such parts — free elimination.

tricks.title: S6 pull-back
tricks.body: Read S6 and ask 'what sentence must come just before it?' — usually the one with Thus/That is why or the summarising judgement. Pin it, then build backwards.

mistakes: Opening with a 'the' sentence whose noun appears nowhere before.
Treating a general statement and an example as interchangeable order.
Missing that 'Now' signals a present-time contrast and must follow the past-time claim.
Placing the conclusion pair (Thus …) in the middle of the chain.
subtopics.notes:
### Why openers are easier to spot than middles
The first part after S1 has to connect to S1 alone, so there is only one link to check. Every other part has to connect to parts you have not placed yet. Settle the opener first, then build the chain from it.

The fastest test is the **orphan test**. Read each part as if it came straight after S1. A part fails if it contains:
- a pronoun whose noun appears only in another part ('It sat down beside the principal' when the dog is introduced in a middle part),
- a 'this/these + noun' that S1 does not supply ('This ability...', 'These halls...'),
- a follow-on word such as 'also', 'even', 'others', 'too', 'in the morning'.
Usually two or three parts fail, and the opener is obvious.

### Connectors inside a PQRS item
Connector words (However, Yet, But, Therefore) cannot open a free paragraph. In a PQRS item, though, S1 is already there, so a connector part can follow S1 directly when S1 is the claim it responds to. 'Many students think maths is only for the gifted. However, this belief is not true.' — here 'However, this belief' is the right first part, because 'this belief' is S1.

So the real rule is: **a connector follows the claim it turns on.** If that claim is S1, the connector part comes first; if the claim is in another part, it comes right after that part.

### Closers and S6
The Close part usually carries a signal: therefore, thus, hence, clearly, that is why, the need of the hour, the next step. Two checks confirm it:
1. It must follow everything it summarises — 'Hence, experts warn the species could vanish' needs the threats listed first.
2. It must lead naturally into S6. If S6 is itself a conclusion ('Saving it will need urgent action'), the Close part prepares for it.

### General before specific
When two parts could both open, choose the more general one. 'Each region cooks with what grows around it' comes before 'In Kerala, for example...'. An example needs the claim it illustrates. The words 'for example', 'in Punjab', 'during deep sleep' mark specific parts.

### Order of work
1. Orphan test on all four parts -> the opener.
2. Signal words -> the closer.
3. The two middle parts -> one pair decides.

### Quick revision
- Orphan test: pronoun, 'this + noun', also/even/others -> cannot open.
- A connector follows the claim it turns on — which can be S1 itself.
- Closers: therefore, thus, hence, clearly, that is why — they follow everything they summarise.
- General claim before its example; 'for example' is never first.
- Opener, then closer, then one pair for the middle.

patterns.name: Orphan test for the opener
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three parts begin with pronouns or 'this + noun' (It sat down..., This ability..., Their protest...), and only one part introduces a new noun.
patterns.logic:
1. Read each part as if it came straight after S1.
2. Remove every part whose pronoun or 'this + noun' has nothing to refer to in S1.
3. The part that remains is the opener; attach the pronoun parts to it.

*Why it works:* a pronoun cannot come before the noun it refers to, so the part that introduces the noun must come first.

example.q: S1: The morning assembly began as usual. Parts: Suddenly, a stray dog walked onto the stage / It sat down beside the principal / ...
example.solution: 'It' fails the orphan test (S1 has no dog), so the 'stray dog' part opens and the 'It' part follows it directly.

patterns.name: Connector follows the claim it turns on
patterns.howToSpot: One part begins with However/But/Yet and S1 (or another part) states the claim it disputes.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the claim the connector answers ('this belief', 'the same device').
2. If the claim is S1, the connector part comes first; otherwise it follows the part that makes the claim.
3. Place its example or support right after it.

*Why it works:* a contrast needs something to contrast with, and that must come just before it.

example.q: S1: Many students think maths is only for the gifted. Part: However, this belief is simply not true.
example.solution: 'This belief' is S1's claim, so the However part comes first; the research and the example support it; 'Therefore' closes.

patterns.name: Closing signal part
patterns.howToSpot: One part carries hence/therefore/clearly/that is why, or proposes a solution, and S6 is a final judgement.
patterns.logic:
1. Mark the part with the closing signal.
2. Check that everything it summarises comes before it.
3. Place it last, just before S6, and order the rest.

*Why it works:* a conclusion depends on all the points before it, so it can only go at the end.

example.q: S1: Traffic jams waste millions of hours. Parts include: Clearly, the answer lies in moving people, not vehicles.
example.solution: 'Clearly' concludes the cause, the failed fix and the contrast, so it sits just before S6.

patterns.name: General before specific
patterns.howToSpot: One part makes a general claim and one or two begin with 'for example', 'in Kerala', 'during deep sleep', or name a particular case.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the general claim that the specific parts illustrate.
2. Place it before its examples.
3. Pair the examples ('for example' ... 'on the other hand').

*Why it works:* an example only makes sense after the claim it illustrates.

example.q: S1: Indian cuisine changes every few hundred kilometres. Parts: Each region cooks with what grows around it / In Kerala, for example... / In Punjab, on the other hand...
example.solution: The general part leads, then Kerala, then Punjab ('on the other hand' needs the first example), then the summary.

subtopics.title: Mandatory pairs: the links that never break
subtopics.concept:
Rearrangement questions are solved through 2–3 unbreakable links. Learn the pair types:

| Pair type | Example | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Noun → Pronoun | '…the crow.' → 'It flew away.' | pronoun follows its noun immediately or near |
| A → The | '…found a piece of bread.' → 'The bread was sweet.' | 'the' needs the earlier 'a' |
| Cause → Effect | '…machines replaced workers.' → 'This led to unemployment.' | 'This/As a result/Therefore' follows cause |
| Contrast pair | '…banned plastic.' → 'Yet people use it.' | Yet/But/However follows the claim |
| General → Specific | 'Museums store history.' → 'Coins, weapons and paintings …' | example after claim |
| Question → Answer | 'Who will bell the cat?' → 'No one came forward.' | answer follows question |
| Name → Role | '…the eldest villager.' → 'He told stories.' | role description follows introduction |

**Pronoun gender and number are free checks:** a chain that has 'he' pointing at 'the boys' is broken. So is 'its' pointing at 'workers'.

**The definite-article cascade:** once a noun appears with 'a', every later mention uses 'the' — so inside the options, scan which part mentions the noun FIRST with 'a'; that part precedes all 'the + same noun' parts.

**Demonstrative pairs:** 'this decision, that scheme, these problems' — the demonstrative locks onto an earlier abstract noun (decision, scheme, problems). Find the noun, find the pair.

tricks.title: Noun-first scan
tricks.body: List the nouns/pronouns across P, Q, R, S. Circle pronouns and 'the'-nouns; draw arrows to the part that introduces each noun. The arrows ARE the answer skeleton.

tricks.title: This/That noun hunt
tricks.body: For every 'this + abstract noun', find which part contains that abstract noun. The order is forced.

tricks.title: a→the cascade
tricks.body: The part containing 'a + noun' must come before every part containing 'the + same noun'. Instant orderer for food-and-trick passages.

mistakes: Breaking a noun→pronoun pair for the sake of time markers.
Missing the second mention of a noun ('the bread' after 'a piece of bread').
Letting an effect part precede its cause because the cause reads well alone.
Ignoring number agreement in pronoun chains (its/their).
subtopics.notes:
### Not all links are equally strong
A mandatory pair is two parts that must sit side by side. Rank the links you find, and trust the strong ones first:

| Strength | Link | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Very strong | Personal pronoun -> its only noun | a stray dog ... **It** sat down |
| Very strong | a + noun -> the + same noun | **a small bag** ... **The bag** was full of gold |
| Very strong | this/these/such + noun -> the part that names it | a huge challenge ... **this challenge** |
| Strong | As a result / Because of this / This has led to -> the cause | sewage flows in ... **This has** filled |
| Strong | Place words: There, Here, Inside -> the place named | moved to the US ... **There** she earned a doctorate |
| Medium | But / Yet / However -> the claim it contradicts | reach in seconds ... **Yet** a letter carries... |
| Weak | Same topic, no grammar link | two parts both about trains |

When two links point to different orders, the stronger one wins. Never break a pronoun pair to satisfy a weak topic link.

### Hidden pointers
Some pointer words are easy to miss:
- **also, too, as well** — the part is a second item and needs a first one before it.
- **Others, Some, the rest** — 'Others have built study halls' needs 'Many now lend e-books' before it.
- **Even** — 'Even the principal could not keep a straight face' needs others laughing first.
- **the same, such, so many** — they point back to a noun or number already given.

### Pairs join into chains
Pairs link up: if P-S is a pair and S-Q is a pair, then P-S-Q is one block of three. Most items are designed so that pairs cover three of the four parts and one more fact places the last part. Write the blocks down as you find them — PS, SQ -> PSQ — and the answer is almost complete.

### Checking a pair
Read the two parts together aloud. A true pair reads as one smooth thought. A false pair makes you ask 'which one?' or 'what is this about?' Check number and gender too: 'its' cannot refer to 'workers', and 'she' cannot refer to 'the farmer' if the farmer is a man.

### Contrast pairs need care
'But', 'Yet' and 'However' are only medium-strength links, because the claim they contradict can sometimes be in S1 rather than in a part. Confirm with the content: 'Yet a letter carries something a message cannot' contrasts with the speed of messages, so it must come right after the part about emails.

### Quick revision
- Rank links: pronoun, a->the, this + noun, as a result, place word > contrast > same topic.
- Hidden pointers: also, others, even, such, the same.
- Pairs join into blocks (PS + SQ = PSQ); two or three blocks usually decide the item.
- Read the pair together; check number and gender.
- The stronger link always wins.

patterns.name: Noun -> pronoun / place-word pair
patterns.howToSpot: One part names a person, animal or place; another begins with He/She/It/There referring to it.
patterns.logic:
1. List each pronoun or place word and find the only part that names what it refers to.
2. Join those two parts as a block.
3. Check number and gender (she -> the science teacher, not Ravi).

*Why it works:* a pronoun has to come after its noun, and usually straight after it.

example.q: S1: Ravi found an injured sparrow. Parts: He carried it to the science teacher / She cleaned its wing / ...
example.solution: 'She' can only be the science teacher, so the two parts form a pair.

patterns.name: a -> the pair
patterns.howToSpot: A noun appears first with a/an in one part (a small bag, a small room) and with 'the' in another (The bag, the room).
patterns.logic:
1. Scan for nouns that appear twice.
2. The part with 'a + noun' comes before every part with 'the + same noun'.
3. If the 'the' part adds detail about the object, place it directly after.

*Why it works:* English introduces a thing with 'a' and refers back to it with 'the'.

example.q: Parts: the old man left a small bag on the doorstep / The bag was full of gold coins.
example.solution: 'a small bag' introduces it; 'The bag' refers back, so the order is fixed.

patterns.name: this / these + abstract noun
patterns.howToSpot: A part begins with 'this challenge', 'this effort', 'this system', 'this decline', and exactly one other part describes that challenge, effort or system.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the abstract noun after 'this'.
2. Find the part that describes it without naming it that way.
3. Join them; a chain of 'this' words can link three parts.

*Why it works:* 'this + noun' sums up the idea just before it.

example.q: Parts: Keeping so many trains on time is a huge challenge / To meet this challenge, the railways track trains by satellite / This system shows every engine's position.
example.solution: Challenge -> this challenge -> this system: a chain of three.

patterns.name: Contrast pair (claim -> but / yet / however)
patterns.howToSpot: One part begins with But/Yet/However and contradicts something — speed vs feeling, promise vs suitability.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify exactly what the contrast part contradicts.
2. Place it directly after the part that says that, or after S1 if S1 says it.
3. The explanation of the contrast follows it.

*Why it works:* a contrast only makes sense straight after the claim it contradicts.

example.q: Parts: Emails reach people in seconds / Yet a letter carries something a message cannot / The handwriting and the paper bring the writer closer.
example.solution: Speed claim -> 'Yet' contrast -> what the something is: a fixed chain.

subtopics.title: Time-sequence chains
subtopics.concept:
Narrative rearrangements (stories, incidents, history) run on the clock. Fix the chain with:

| Marker | Position signal |
|---|---|
| One day / Long ago / In 1947 / Last winter | earliest event |
| Soon / Then / After that / Meanwhile | next events |
| By midnight / By dawn / Within a week | result-time of the ongoing event |
| The next morning / The following day | day boundary |
| Now / Today / These days | present contrast, near the end |
| Ever since / Since then | after the turning point |

**Build the timeline before touching options:** number the events inside P, Q, R, S (e.g. flood → homes flooded → villagers moved → boats ferried → rescue arrived → normal life). The letter string is just the timeline written in the parts' labels.

**Verb-tense cross-check:** past continuous often paints the background (was raining), simple past the events (came, fell), past perfect the earlier events (had left). A chain that puts a past-perfect event AFTER the simple-past event it caused is broken.

**The day-boundary trick:** 'That night … By dawn …' — any 'by + time' part usually belongs after the action it caps, not before. Options often place 'By midnight' first; it caps the flooding, so it follows the flooding sentence.

tricks.title: Timeline first
tricks.body: Write the 4–6 events as a numbered list, then map numbers to letters. The string writes itself.

tricks.title: Tense radar
tricks.body: Past perfect = earlier; past continuous = background; simple past = the event line. Use tenses to order events when time words are missing.

tricks.title: By-time capping
tricks.body: 'By midnight/By dawn' closes the phase it describes — it follows, never opens, the event chain.

mistakes: Placing 'Now/Today' early in a story that ends in the present.
Ordering by the order the parts are listed, not by the events' clock.
Ignoring 'the next morning' — a hard day-boundary marker.
Letting a result-time phrase open the chain.
subtopics.notes:
### Three layers of time
A narrative item gives you time information at three levels. Use as many as you need:
1. **Markers** — dates and time words: Last December, In 2008, A few days later, That night, By dawn, The next morning, Today.
2. **Tense** — past perfect (had left) for earlier events, simple past for the main events, present (Today, only tourists climb...) for the end.
3. **Cause and effect** — the fire must start before the engines arrive; the lander must fail before it is redesigned.
Markers are the most reliable. When they are missing, use tense; when tense does not help, use cause and effect.

### Relative markers need an anchor
'Eleven years later', 'A few days later', 'Within ten minutes of the restart', 'On the eighth day' all measure from an earlier event. They cannot come first. Find the event they count from and place them after it: 'Eleven years later' needs 'In 2008'; 'the restart' needs 'half-time'.

### By-phrases close a phase
'By dawn, the flames had been put out.' 'By the final whistle, we had won.' A by-phrase describes where a stretch of action ended up, so it follows the actions inside that stretch. Setters often place it first in the wrong options.

### Flashbacks in the past perfect
'When Anil reached the station, the platform was empty. The express had left ten minutes earlier. He had missed it because he had overslept.' The past perfect parts explain the scene, and the story returns to the simple past afterwards ('Cursing his bad luck, he checked the board'). Keep the flashback parts together, directly after the scene they explain.

### Process and instruction passages
Recipes, procedures and application steps use **First -> Next / Then -> After that -> Finally**. When the markers are partly missing, use what each step needs: you cannot book an appointment before registering, and the officials cannot check documents before the appointment exists. 'At the appointment' needs a part that mentions booking it.

### Biography and history
Lives and events run in date order, but look for pointer words too: 'There she earned a doctorate' needs the part naming the country; 'Her second mission' needs the first one. Exam biographies often skip years, so rely on 'first', 'second', 'later' and 'then' as well as dates.

### Quick revision
- Use markers first, then tense, then cause and effect.
- 'Eleven years later', 'a few days later' and 'the restart' need an earlier event before them.
- By-phrases (by dawn, by the final whistle) come after the actions they sum up.
- Past perfect = flashback; keep those parts together, straight after the scene.
- Processes: each step needs the one before it — you cannot book before you register.

patterns.name: Explicit time and date markers
patterns.howToSpot: Parts carry dates or time words: Last December, In 2008, Eleven years later, In August 2023, As soon as they reached.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline every time word.
2. Place fixed dates in order; attach each relative marker after its anchor.
3. Fill in any part without a marker by cause and effect.

*Why it works:* the markers put the events in order before you even read the options.

example.q: Parts: In 2008, Chandrayaan-1 ... / Eleven years later, Chandrayaan-2's lander crashed / Scientists studied the failure / In August 2023, Chandrayaan-3 landed.
example.solution: 2008 -> 'eleven years later' -> 'the failure' -> 2023: the markers and one pointer word fix the order.

patterns.name: By-phrases and day boundaries
patterns.howToSpot: One part begins with By dawn / By the final whistle / By midnight, or with That night / The next morning.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the actions the by-phrase sums up and place it after them.
2. Place day-boundary parts (the next morning) after everything from the day before.
3. Check that S6 continues from the last part.

*Why it works:* a by-phrase describes the result of the actions before it, so it can never come first.

example.q: S1: A fire broke out late on Saturday night. Parts: shopkeepers rushed out / engines arrived within twenty minutes / By dawn, the flames were out / Later that morning, officials counted the damage.
example.solution: People nearby act first, then the engines; 'By dawn' sums up the firefighting; 'later that morning' comes after dawn.

patterns.name: Tense as a clock (past perfect flashback)
patterns.howToSpot: Parts mix had + V3 (had left, had built, had attacked) with simple past and present; there are few time words.
patterns.logic:
1. Past perfect parts = earlier events or background; keep them together in order.
2. Simple past parts continue the main story after them.
3. Present-tense parts (Today...) come last.

*Why it works:* tense shows the order of events even when there are no time words.

example.q: S1: The old fort stood silent. Parts: a king had built it / armies had attacked it / over time the route shifted / today only tourists climb it.
example.solution: had built -> had attacked -> simple past 'shifted' -> present 'Today'.

patterns.name: Process steps
patterns.howToSpot: The passage explains how to do something (a paper boat, a passport application) with First/Next/Then/Finally or steps that depend on each other.
patterns.logic:
1. Use First/Finally to fix the ends.
2. For steps without markers, ask which step each one needs before it.
3. A step that mentions something (the appointment) comes after the step that creates it.

*Why it works:* each step depends on the one before, so the order is forced.

example.q: Parts: registers on the portal / After paying the fee, books an appointment / At the appointment, officials check documents / A police verification follows.
example.solution: Register -> pay and book -> the appointment -> verification: each step needs the one before it.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: elimination, budget and Tier 2 jumbles
subtopics.concept:
**Budget:** Tier 1 allots roughly one rearrangement item per shift — attempt in 35–45 seconds. Tier 2 adds longer paragraph jumbles (5–6 sentences) and sentence-order-in-paragraph items; allow 60–75 seconds there.

**Partial-answer elimination** — the meta-skill: option strings share prefixes and suffixes. Eliminate in layers:
1. Which parts can open the middle? (ban pronoun/connector openers) → kills 2 options.
2. Which pair is mandatory (noun→pronoun)? → kills 1–2 more.
3. Verify the survivor against S6.
Even with only partial certainty you reach one string — full-chain certainty is not required.

**If two strings survive:** find the ONE part whose position differs, and test only that part against its neighbours (does its pronoun have a noun? does its 'therefore' have a cause?). Local tests settle local differences.

**For Tier 2 paragraph jumbles without fixed ends:** find the independent opener (no pronoun/connector), then the pair with the strongest link (usually 'a'→'the' or noun→pronoun), then extend. Odd-sentence-out items use the same skill in reverse — four sentences share a theme; the fifth touches it but never uses its key noun.

**Daily plan:** 5 rearrangements a day with the pairs written out before checking answers. After two weeks, scan-tagging (openers, connectors, demonstratives) runs automatically and the item becomes a 30-second free mark.

tricks.title: Layered elimination
tricks.body: Layer 1: opener ban. Layer 2: mandatory pair. Layer 3: S6 check. Each layer is one question; two layers usually finish the item.

tricks.title: Local-difference test
tricks.body: Surviving strings differ in one part's position. Isolate that part and test only its two neighbours.

tricks.title: Odd-sentence radar
tricks.body: For odd-one-out items, mark each sentence's KEY noun. Four share it; the impostor only orbits it.

mistakes: Spending 90 seconds building the full chain when two eliminations would finish the item.
Refusing to mark an answer with partial certainty — elimination already gives the string.
Reading the options before reading P, Q, R, S (backwards order wastes the read).
In odd-one-out, choosing the least-familiar sentence instead of the one missing the key noun.
subtopics.notes:
### A 40-second routine
1. **Read S1 and S6 (5 s).** Note the subject and what S6 refers back to.
2. **Tag the parts (15 s).** Mark pronouns, 'this + noun', connectors, time words and closing signals.
3. **Fix one end and one pair (10 s).** The opener (orphan test) or the closer (S6 pull-back), plus the strongest pair.
4. **Eliminate (10 s).** Remove every string that breaks that end or pair; usually one is left.
You do not need to be sure of the whole paragraph — you only need to rule out three strings.

### Jumbles with no fixed ends
Without S1 and S6 you lose both clamps, so:
- Find the **independent sentence**: no pronoun pointing back, no connector, no 'this + noun', no 'also'. It opens.
- Find the **strongest pair** (a->the, pronoun, this + noun) and extend the chain from the opener.
- The **closer** is the part with a conclusion signal or a 'this + noun' that sums up the whole problem ('close this gap').
Setters often write two sentences that look independent. Choose the more general one, or the one the other refers to.

### First-sentence and last-sentence questions
Some papers ask only which sentence comes first or last. Do not arrange all four:
- **First:** apply the orphan test to every sentence. The one that passes is the answer. If two pass, the more general one wins.
- **Last:** look for the sentence that sums up ('Such conveniences...', 'Greed had cost him...') or completes the final step of a story or process, and check that nothing else must follow it.
This takes 20-30 seconds.

### When two strings survive
If you are left with two strings such as QRPS and QPRS, find the parts that are in different positions (here R and P) and test only those neighbours. Does P's 'But it has also' need R's 'This has made life easier' before it? Checking one small difference is faster than rereading the whole paragraph.

### Common traps
- **Nearly-right strings:** the wrong options often keep the correct opener and closer and swap two middle parts. Check the middle pair even when both ends match.
- **Topic similarity:** two parts about the same subject are not necessarily a pair. Only grammar links (pronoun, a->the, this + noun, connector) are reliable.
- **A strong-sounding first line:** a part with a date ('In August 2023...') feels like an opener but may be the end of the story. Check the anchors.

### Quick revision
- Routine: read S1 and S6 -> tag the parts -> fix one end and one pair -> eliminate.
- No fixed ends: independent sentence first, strongest pair next, summary last.
- First/last questions: orphan test for first; summary or final step for last.
- Two strings left: test only the parts that differ.
- Grammar links beat topic similarity; dates can be endings, not openers.

patterns.name: Paragraph jumble with no fixed ends
patterns.howToSpot: Four sentences labelled P, Q, R, S with no S1 or S6; the options are four-letter strings.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the independent sentence (no pronoun, connector, 'this + noun' or 'also') — it opens.
2. Attach the strongest pair to it.
3. The summary or 'this + noun' sentence closes.

*Why it works:* without S1 and S6, the opener has to be the one sentence that needs nothing before it.

example.q: P: At the same time, many families go hungry. Q: Every year, millions of tonnes of food are wasted. R: Better cold storage could close this gap. S: Much of it rots in storage.
example.solution: Q is the only independent sentence; S ('Much of it') follows; P adds the contrast; R ('this gap') closes: QSPR.

patterns.name: Which sentence comes first?
patterns.howToSpot: The options are just the labels P, Q, R, S and the question asks for the opening sentence.
patterns.logic:
1. Apply the orphan test to each sentence.
2. Remove every sentence with a pronoun, 'this + noun', a connector or a relative time marker.
3. The remaining sentence is the answer.

*Why it works:* you only need the opener, so arranging the other three is wasted time.

example.q: P: Their destination was Dandi. Q: On reaching the sea, he picked up salt. R: In 1930, Gandhiji set out from Sabarmati Ashram. S: This simple act inspired millions.
example.solution: P ('Their'), Q ('he') and S ('This act') all point back; R introduces Gandhiji — R is first.

patterns.name: Which sentence comes last?
patterns.howToSpot: The options are just the labels and the question asks for the closing sentence.
patterns.logic:
1. Look for the sentence that sums up ('Such conveniences...', 'Greed had cost him...') or completes the last step of a story.
2. Check that no other sentence needs to follow it (nothing else points back to it).
3. Confirm by building the chain backwards.

*Why it works:* the last sentence is the one that refers back to others but that nothing refers back to.

example.q: P: Others follow this trail and carry the food home. Q: Each colony divides work. R: When a worker finds food, it leaves a trail. S: Ants are very organised.
example.solution: P's 'this trail' needs R, and nothing refers back to P — P is last.

patterns.name: Two strings left: test only the difference
patterns.howToSpot: You have ruled out two strings, and the remaining two differ only in the positions of two neighbouring parts.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the two surviving strings one above the other.
2. Identify the two parts that switch places.
3. Test only that link: does one of them point back to the other?

*Why it works:* the correct string and the closest wrong one differ at a single point, so testing that point decides the item.

example.q: Survivors QRPS and QPRS. R: This has made life easier. P: But it has also created chances for fraud.
example.solution: 'But it has also' needs the benefit in R before it, so R comes before P: QRPS.

pyqPatterns.pattern: PQRS rearrangement with fixed S1 and S6
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Sentence 1 and sentence 6 are given; the four middle parts are labelled P, Q, R, S and the options are four-letter strings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read S1 and S6 first. Tag the parts (Lead, Support, Turn, Close), find the two strongest pairs, fix the first or last part, then remove every string that breaks a pair. Usually one string is left.

example.q: S1: Stubble burning chokes north India every winter. Parts: farmers burn the straw / the smoke drifts to the cities / this thick smog sends thousands to hospital / some states now pay for straw-cutting machines. S6: Subsidies for such machines must be extended.
example.solution: Cause -> 'The smoke' -> 'This thick smog' -> response; S6's 'such machines' puts the response part last.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four to six sentences with no S1 or S6; options are letter strings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the one independent sentence (no pronoun, connector, 'this + noun' or 'also') — it opens. Attach pairs to it and put the summary or 'this + noun' sentence last.

example.q: P: Their numbers, however, have been falling. Q: Pesticides are the main reason for this decline. R: Farmers planting hedges are helping to reverse it. S: Honeybees help produce a third of our food.
example.solution: S is the only independent sentence -> P ('Their') -> Q ('this decline') -> R ('reverse it'): SPQR.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Opener: orphan test and the connector rule
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Several parts begin with a pronoun, 'this + noun' or a connector; only one introduces a new noun.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read each part as if it came straight after S1. Remove the ones whose pronoun or 'this + noun' has nothing to refer to in S1. A However/But part may open only when it answers S1 itself.

example.q: S1: Many people believe that eating fat makes you fat. Which part follows S1: 'However, this belief is only partly true' or 'What it does not need is excess sugar'?
example.solution: 'This belief' is S1's claim, so the However part follows S1; 'What it does not need' needs 'the body needs...' before it.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Closer: conclusion signal and S6 pull-back
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One part carries therefore / hence / clearly, or S6 begins with a pronoun, 'such' or 'these'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Circle what S6 points back to — the part that supplies it is last. A part with a conclusion signal comes after everything it sums up.

example.q: S6: Such a response has encouraged the colony to open a reading corner. Which part is last: 'Within a month, two hundred people had borrowed books' or 'Volunteers arranged the books on these shelves'?
example.solution: 'Such a response' = two hundred borrowers, so the borrowing part is last.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Mandatory pair (pronoun, a -> the, this + noun, contrast)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two parts are joined by a pointer: It/She/There, a bag -> the bag, this problem, Yet/But, also/others/too.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write each pair as a block (PS, SQ -> PSQ). Trust grammar links over topic links; two or three blocks usually leave one string.

example.q: Parts: 'the traveller left a small clay pot on the doorstep' / 'Inside the pot, the farmer found a bag of seeds'.
example.solution: 'a small clay pot' -> 'the pot': the 'a' part must come directly before the 'the' part.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Parts carry dates, 'later', 'that evening', 'By Wednesday morning', or mix past perfect with simple past.
pyqPatterns.approach: Place fixed dates in order; attach each relative marker to its anchor. By-phrases come after the actions they sum up. Past perfect parts are flashbacks; present tense ('Today') is last.

example.q: Parts: 'Within hours, trucks were stuck' / 'Army teams reached them that evening' / 'By Wednesday morning, a lane was cleared' / 'Later that day, vehicles were escorted down'.
example.solution: hours -> evening -> by Wednesday morning -> later that day.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options are single labels (P, Q, R, S) and the question asks only for the first or the last sentence.
pyqPatterns.approach: First: the sentence that passes the orphan test (more general if two pass; check for hidden pointers like 'similarly'). Last: the sentence that points back to others but that nothing points back to.

example.q: P: He buried it in a hole. Q: A miser bought a lump of gold. R: Every night he dug it up. S: A thief, who had been watching him, stole the gold. Which is last?
example.solution: S — the thief had watched the nightly digging, and nothing refers back to the theft.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Five sentences are given and one does not belong to the paragraph formed by the others.
pyqPatterns.approach: Build the chain of pairs among the sentences; the one that links to none of them (a new topic, or a different time and person) is the odd one.

example.q: Sentences on UPI payments, QR codes at stalls, scanning to pay, overspending — and one on the history of coins in the Mughal era.
example.solution: The Mughal-coins sentence has no pointer to or from the others and belongs to a different time — it is the odd one.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Sentence order inside a cloze / paragraph completion
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A paragraph has a missing sentence or a sentence to be placed at a gap; options are sentences or positions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Apply the same links: the missing sentence must pick up the pronoun or 'this + noun' after the gap and continue the idea before it.

example.q: Gap between 'Emails reach people in seconds.' and 'The handwriting brings the writer closer.'
example.solution: The gap needs a contrast that introduces what the handwriting explains: 'Yet a letter carries something a message cannot.'

solvedExamples.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The village celebrated its first electricity connection. **P:** The children had never seen a bulb glow. **Q:** That night, every street hummed with excitement. **R:** The elders remembered decades of darkness. **S:** It was, everyone agreed, the beginning of a new era. **6.** The panchayat promised more changes soon.
solvedExamples.solution: After S1 (celebration announced), **R** opens the memories — elders remembering 'decades of darkness' explains the celebration. **P** follows with the children (another group), **Q** takes us to 'that night' (the event itself), and **S** ('It was … the beginning') is the summary judgement closing before S6's promise. RPQS.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Openers: R and P are recall-pairs (elders/children); Q's 'that night' pins the event; S's 'It was' summary sits last.

solvedExamples.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Ravi found a wallet on the bus. **P:** Inside it he found some cash and an ID card. **Q:** The card carried an address in the same city. **R:** The next morning, he returned it to its owner. **S:** The owner was overjoyed and offered a reward. **6.** Ravi refused the reward with a smile.
solvedExamples.solution: Chain: 'Inside **it**' needs the wallet (S1) → **P**. 'The **card**' needs the ID card mentioned → **Q**. 'The **next morning**' moves time forward → **R**. 'The **owner**' needs the returning (owner only exists after return) → **S**. Then S6. PQRS.
solvedExamples.shortcut: a→the cascade: wallet→it, card→the card; owner appears only after returning.

solvedExamples.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The rains failed for the third year. **P:** By midnight the wells had gone dry. **Q:** Farmers began selling their cattle cheaply. **R:** As a result, the district was declared drought-hit. **S:** The government opened relief camps soon after. **6.** Recovery, however, took two full years.
solvedExamples.solution: Timeline: wells dry at midnight (**P**) → farmers sell cattle (**Q**) → 'As a result' of these hardships, drought declared (**R**) → relief camps 'soon after' (**S**) → recovery (**S6**). QPRS: the 'by midnight' caps the water crisis, selling follows, the result-declaration needs both as its cause.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'As a result' follows its causes; 'By + time' caps the phase; 'soon after' rides behind the declaration.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The river had overflowed its banks. **P:** The villagers moved to higher ground with their cattle. **Q:** Water entered hundreds of homes by midnight. **R:** Rescue teams reached only the next morning. **S:** Boats carried families to temporary shelters. **6.** Life returned to normal after a week.
practice.solution: Timeline: homes flooded **by midnight** (**Q** caps the flooding) → villagers moved (**P**) → boats ferried them (**S**) → rescue arrived 'the next morning' (**R**) → normal life (**S6**). QPSR.
practice.shortcut: By-time caps the flooding; day-boundary marker ends the chain.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Reading books is a habit worth cultivating. **P:** It improves vocabulary and concentration. **Q:** Children who read daily perform better in school. **R:** Unfortunately, television has replaced books in many homes. **S:** Parents should therefore encourage reading from an early age. **6.** A nation of readers must begin at home.
practice.solution: 'It' needs the noun from S1 (reading) → **P** opens. **Q** gives the school evidence. **R** contrasts ('Unfortunately') with the good run. **S** concludes with 'therefore' just before S6. PQRS.
practice.shortcut: Pronoun orphan test opens P; therefore-clause closes the chain.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Manual work is steadily giving way to machines. **P:** This has led to unemployment in some sectors. **Q:** But new jobs have appeared in technology. **R:** Workers must therefore learn new skills. **S:** Machines work faster and never tire. **6.** Adaptability is the only security left.
practice.solution: **S** explains S1 (why machines replace work) → **P** ('This has led to') draws the unemployment consequence → **Q** ('But') contrasts with new jobs → **R** ('therefore') concludes. SPQR.
practice.shortcut: Cause-effect pair S→P; contrast Q; therefore-conclusion R.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** India's cities are growing at a breathtaking pace. **P:** This puts heavy pressure on housing and transport. **Q:** New settlements are spilling beyond city limits. **R:** The government has launched new urban schemes in reply. **S:** Slums are spreading along every highway. **6.** Whether they succeed, only time will tell.
practice.solution: **P** follows S1 (growth → pressure, 'This' = growth) → **Q** details the spill-over → **S** shows the slum result on the ground → **R** brings the reply (schemes) just before S6's verdict. PQSR.
practice.shortcut: Demonstrative pair S1→P; ground-level detail before the response; R is the closing action.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A museum is a storehouse of history. **P:** Each artefact tells a story of its time. **Q:** Visitors can see weapons, coins and paintings there. **R:** Curators work hard to preserve these treasures. **S:** Some pieces are thousands of years old. **6.** A trip to a museum is a walk through time.
practice.solution: **Q** (specific exhibits, 'there' = museum) → **P** (each artefact = those exhibits) → **S** (their age) → **R** ('these treasures' = the pieces) → S6. QPSR.
practice.shortcut: General→specific: claim, examples, then 'these treasures' needs the pieces before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The sun had set behind the hills. **P:** Soon the stars appeared one by one. **Q:** A cool breeze began to blow. **R:** The villagers gathered under the banyan tree. **S:** The eldest among them told stories of the old days. **6.** Night after night, this ritual continued.
practice.solution: Scene continues: breeze (**Q**) → gathering (**R**, 'them' = villagers) → stars appear (**P**, 'Soon') → the eldest tells stories (**S**) → ritual (**S6**). QRPS.
practice.shortcut: 'Among them' needs the villagers first; 'Soon' rides after the gathering.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Mountaineering is not a mere adventure sport. **P:** It teaches discipline and teamwork. **Q:** Climbers roped together must trust one another completely. **R:** One careless step can end a life. **S:** That is why preparation matters more than courage. **6.** The mountain forgives nothing.
practice.solution: 'It' = mountaineering → **P**. **Q** explains the teamwork claim (roped climbers). **R** gives the danger ('one careless step') that makes preparation vital → **S** ('That is why') concludes. PQRS.
practice.shortcut: That-is-why pair needs the danger sentence R immediately before S.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Plastic waste has become a global menace. **P:** It blocks drains and kills cattle that swallow it. **Q:** Many governments have banned single-use plastic bags. **R:** Yet people continue to use them for convenience. **S:** Awareness, not merely bans, is the need of the hour. **6.** Behaviour must change before laws can succeed.
practice.solution: 'It' = plastic waste → **P** (harm). **Q** (response: bans). **R** ('Yet') contrasts — usage continues. **S** concludes ('need of the hour') before S6. PQRS.
practice.shortcut: Yet-clause must follow the ban; conclusion word flags the final slot.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** One day, a hungry crow found a piece of bread. **P:** The crow flew to a tree with it. **Q:** A clever fox saw it from below and wanted the bread. **R:** The fox began to praise the crow's beautiful voice. **S:** The foolish crow sang at once, dropping the bread. **6.** The fox picked it up and trotted away.
practice.solution: Crow flies up with the bread (**P**, 'it' = bread) → fox sees it (**Q**, 'it' = the scene) → fox flatters (**R**) → crow sings and drops it (**S**) → fox grabs it (**S6**). PQRS — the a→the and it-chains run through every joint.
practice.shortcut: Pronoun chains: bread→it, and the fox must see before praising.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** There was a time when letters were the only bridge between families. **P:** People waited eagerly for the postman's knock. **Q:** Now instant messages flash across screens. **R:** Yet something precious died with the waiting. **S:** Few would trade speed for that sweetness today. **6.** Or perhaps they already have.
practice.solution: Past scene: waiting for the postman (**P**) → present contrast 'Now' (**Q**) → 'Yet' laments the lost waiting (**R**) → S concedes the trade, S6 caps the irony. PQRS.
practice.shortcut: Now = present contrast after the past scene; Yet needs Q's speed claim before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Water is the source of all life. **P:** Industries release effluents into the rivers. **Q:** Groundwater levels are falling every year. **R:** We must harvest rainwater without delay. **S:** Cities dump untreated sewage into the same rivers. **6.** Otherwise the taps of tomorrow will run dry.
practice.solution: **P** (industrial pollution) → **S** (city sewage, 'the same rivers' needs P's rivers) → **Q** (falling groundwater completes the crisis) → **R** (the remedy) before S6. PSQR.
practice.shortcut: 'The same rivers' locks S after P; remedy (must) sits last before S6.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Grandmother's kitchen was the heart of our home. **P:** The aroma of spices filled every corner. **Q:** She kneaded dough before sunrise. **R:** Everyone gathered when the meal bell rang. **S:** No restaurant meal could match her cooking. **6.** We still measure every kitchen by hers.
practice.solution: 'She' needs grandmother (S1) → **Q** opens (morning work). **P** follows (aroma from cooking). **R** brings the family at mealtime. **S** delivers the judgement (no match) before S6. QPRS.
practice.shortcut: Pronoun orphan: She must open; judgement sentence S closes.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The Internet has changed education forever. **P:** Students in remote villages now attend world-class lectures. **Q:** Quality no longer depends on location. **R:** However, screen fatigue is a real cost. **S:** Teachers must blend online lessons with offline care. **6.** The classroom of the future will be hybrid.
practice.solution: **P** (village access) → **Q** (the principle it proves) → **R** ('However' cost) → **S** (the blending remedy) → S6 (hybrid future). PQRS.
practice.shortcut: However-clause follows the gains; remedy sentence precedes S6.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The old bridge was declared unsafe last month. **P:** Engineers examined every pillar for a week. **Q:** Traffic was diverted to a longer route. **R:** Repairs began within a fortnight. **S:** Commuters faced long delays at first. **6.** The bridge reopened, stronger than before.
practice.solution: Inspection first (**P**) → diversion (**Q**) → commuters' delays (**S**, consequence of Q) → repairs (**R**) → reopening (**S6**). PQSR.
practice.shortcut: Delays are the child of diversion: Q before S; repairs precede reopening.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A small act of kindness can travel far. **P:** Last winter, a stranger gave his umbrella to a shivering beggar. **Q:** The beggar's smile warmed the whole street. **R:** Such moments cost nothing. **S:** Yet they remain rare in our hurried lives. **6.** Perhaps the umbrella told the whole story.
practice.solution: The story first: umbrella given (**P**) → the smile it caused (**Q**) → general lesson 'Such moments' (**R**) → 'Yet' concession (**S**) → S6. PQRS.
practice.shortcut: Example precedes the 'Such' judgement; Yet-clause closes before S6.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Yoga has become popular across the world. **P:** Many of them say it has lowered their stress. **Q:** Beginners should therefore start under a trained teacher. **R:** Millions now practise it daily in parks and studios. **S:** However, many learn it only from online videos. **6.** A wrong posture can do more harm than good.
practice.solution: Lead **R** continues S1 ('it' = yoga). **P**'s 'Many of them' needs the millions in **R**, giving the pair **R****P**. The Turn **S** ('However') contrasts with these benefits, and the Close **Q** ('therefore') draws the lesson from it. S6's warning about wrong postures follows the advice to find a teacher. **RPSQ**.
practice.shortcut: Lead-Support-Turn-Close: 'them' pair, then However, then therefore.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Online banking has changed how Indians handle money. **P:** But the same convenience has opened doors to fraud. **Q:** Bills can now be paid in seconds from a phone. **R:** Customers must therefore never share their OTP with anyone. **S:** This has saved people countless trips to the branch. **6.** Banks, too, keep repeating this warning.
practice.solution: **Q** gives the Lead fact, and **S**'s 'This has saved' refers to it. **P**'s 'the same convenience' can only come after the benefit is described, and its 'But' turns the argument. **R** is the Close ('therefore') drawn from the fraud risk, and S6's 'this warning' refers back to it. **QSPR**.
practice.shortcut: 'the same convenience' needs the benefit first; S6's 'this warning' fixes the last part.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Stubble burning chokes north India every winter. **P:** Some states now pay farmers to use straw-cutting machines instead. **Q:** The smoke drifts to the cities and mixes with the winter fog. **R:** This thick smog sends thousands to hospital with breathing trouble. **S:** Farmers burn the leftover rice straw to clear their fields quickly. **6.** Subsidies for such machines, experts say, must be extended further.
practice.solution: Problem skeleton. Cause: **S**, straw is burnt. Effect: **Q**, 'The smoke' of that burning. Harm: **R**, 'This thick smog' is the smoke mixed with fog. Response: **P**, machines instead of burning. S6's 'such machines' refers to **P**, so it is last. **SQRP**.
practice.shortcut: Cause -> effect -> harm -> response; 'such machines' in S6 pulls the response to the end.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Mobile phone addiction is rising among teenagers. **P:** Many spend over six hours a day scrolling through short videos. **Q:** Some schools have now introduced phone-free hours to break the habit. **R:** Such constant screen time leaves little room for sleep. **S:** Tired and restless, they then struggle to focus in class. **6.** Early results from these schools are encouraging.
practice.solution: **P** states the problem in numbers. **R**'s 'Such constant screen time' sums up **P**. **S**'s 'Tired' is the effect of lost sleep, so it follows **R**. **Q** is the response, and S6's 'these schools' refers to it. **PRSQ**.
practice.shortcut: 'Such' sums up the part before it; S6's 'these schools' fixes the response last.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Our colony started a small library in an empty garage. **P:** They also kept a register so that anyone could borrow a book for a week. **Q:** Within a month, more than two hundred people had borrowed books. **R:** Residents donated old books and a few steel shelves. **S:** Volunteers arranged the books on these shelves by subject. **6.** Such a response has encouraged the colony to open a reading corner for children.
practice.solution: S6 begins 'Such a response', so the part it refers to — **Q**, two hundred borrowers — must be last. Working back: **P**'s 'They also' refers to the volunteers in **S**, and **S**'s 'these shelves' refers to **R**. **RSPQ**.
practice.shortcut: Start from S6: 'Such a response' = the borrowers, then chain back through 'They also' and 'these shelves'.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Last month, a jewellery shop in our town was robbed. **P:** While one threatened the owner, the other filled a bag with gold chains. **Q:** Two men entered the shop wearing helmets. **R:** The police sent these pictures to every airport and railway station. **S:** A camera across the road recorded their faces as they removed the helmets outside. **6.** The thieves were caught boarding a flight a week later.
practice.solution: S6 says the thieves were caught at an airport, which refers back to **R**, the police alert to airports. **R**'s 'these pictures' needs the camera in **S**. **P**'s 'one ... the other' needs the two men of **Q**. The robbery happens before they walk out, so **P** comes before **S**. **QPSR**.
practice.shortcut: S6 (airport) -> alert part last; 'these pictures' and 'one ... the other' give two pairs.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The Konkan Railway is one of India's most scenic railway lines. **P:** The longest of these tunnels is over 6 km long. **Q:** Monsoon journeys on the line are especially popular with tourists. **R:** Along the way, it passes through more than 90 tunnels. **S:** Its route runs for over 700 km along the western coast. **6.** Waterfalls then appear beside the track at almost every bend.
practice.solution: **S**'s 'Its route' can only point to the railway line in S1, so it comes first. **R**'s 'Along the way' needs that route, and **P**'s 'these tunnels' needs **R**. S6's 'then' means during the monsoon, so **Q** sits just before it. **SRPQ**.
practice.shortcut: S1 hook 'Its route' opens; 'these tunnels' pairs; S6's 'then' pulls the monsoon part last.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Every winter, thousands of flamingos fly to the Rann of Kutch. **P:** They do so because the shallow salt marshes are full of tiny shrimp and algae. **Q:** The birds also build mud-mound nests on the flat islands of the Rann. **R:** Because of this, the region is often called 'Flamingo City'. **S:** This food is what gives the birds their famous pink colour. **6.** Bird-watchers arrive in large numbers to see the colony.
practice.solution: 'They do so' repeats S1's action (flying to the Rann), so **P** must come first. **S**'s 'This food' is the shrimp and algae of **P**. **Q** adds a second fact with 'also', and **R**'s 'Because of this' — the nesting colony — names the place, so **Q****R** is a pair. **PSQR**.
practice.shortcut: 'They do so' is an S1 hook; then two pairs: food and nests.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A young engineer in Assam wanted to build cheap houses for flood-hit families. **P:** The government has now ordered five hundred such houses for riverside villages. **Q:** Because the bamboo is grown locally, each house costs very little. **R:** He designed a bamboo house that stands on stilts above the water level. **S:** Its low cost soon attracted the attention of the state government. **6.** Families moving in say they no longer fear the monsoon.
practice.solution: Every part points back to the one before it: 'He' = the engineer in S1 (**R**); 'the bamboo' = **R**'s bamboo house (**Q**); 'Its low cost' = **Q**'s cheap houses (**S**); 'The government' = the state government in **S** (**P**). A chain of three pairs fixes the whole order. **RQSP**.
practice.shortcut: Pointer chain: He -> the bamboo -> Its low cost -> The government.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Indian households throw away tonnes of old clothes every year. **P:** It sorts them into those that can be worn again and those that cannot. **Q:** The rest are shredded and woven into floor mats. **R:** The wearable ones are washed and given to families in need. **S:** A Delhi start-up now collects these clothes from homes. **6.** These mats are sold to pay for the whole operation.
practice.solution: **P**'s 'It' is the start-up in **S**. **P** makes two groups, and **R** ('The wearable ones') and **Q** ('The rest') take them in order — 'the rest' only makes sense after the first group is mentioned. S6's 'These mats' refers to **Q**, so it is last. **SPRQ**.
practice.shortcut: 'It' pair + 'the wearable ones ... the rest' pair; S6's 'These mats' confirms the end.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The annual science fair opened in our school hall on Friday. **P:** Watching this, the chief guest asked her how long it had taken to build. **Q:** A Class 8 student displayed a robot that sorts dry and wet waste. **R:** It picked up plastic bottles and dropped them into the blue bin. **S:** She replied that it had taken her three months of weekends. **6.** The robot won the first prize.
practice.solution: Orphan test: **R** ('It'), **P** ('Watching this') and **S** ('She replied') all point back to something not in S1. Only **Q** introduces a new noun, so it opens. Then 'It' = the robot, 'this' = the sorting, 'She replied' = the answer to the guest's question. **QRPS**.
practice.shortcut: Three pronoun parts fail the orphan test; the part with 'A Class 8 student' opens.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Our train stopped suddenly in the middle of a forest. **P:** Forest guards arrived and gently freed the little one. **Q:** Only then did we notice that its calf was stuck between the rails. **R:** A large elephant was standing on the tracks ahead. **S:** The driver sounded the horn several times, but it refused to move. **6.** Mother and calf walked slowly back into the trees, and the train moved on.
practice.solution: **R** introduces the elephant, so it passes the orphan test and opens. **S**'s 'it refused' needs the elephant. **Q**'s 'Only then' needs the failed horn in **S**. **P**'s 'the little one' is the calf in **Q**. **RSQP**.
practice.shortcut: New noun opens; 'Only then' follows the failed attempt; 'the little one' = the calf.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The old library in our town was about to be demolished. **P:** Their petition reached the district collector within a week. **Q:** She collected signatures from over three thousand residents. **R:** He ordered that the building be repaired instead. **S:** A retired teacher refused to accept this. **6.** Today the library is busier than ever.
practice.solution: **S**'s 'this' is the planned demolition in S1, so it passes the orphan test. **Q**'s 'She' is the teacher, **P**'s 'Their petition' is the residents' signatures, and **R**'s 'He' is the collector. Each part points back to the one before it. **SQPR**.
practice.shortcut: 'this' pointing to S1 is allowed; She -> Their -> He chain follows.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Many people believe that eating fat makes you fat. **P:** A sensible diet should therefore cut sugar rather than fat. **Q:** However, this belief is only partly true. **R:** What it does not need is the excess sugar in sweets and soft drinks. **S:** The body, in fact, needs the healthy fats found in nuts and fish. **6.** Such a diet also keeps the heart healthy.
practice.solution: 'This belief' is S1's claim, so the However part **Q** follows S1 directly. **R**'s 'What it does not need' contrasts with **S**'s 'needs', so they form a pair. **P**'s 'therefore' draws the conclusion, and S6's 'Such a diet' refers to it. **QSRP**.
practice.shortcut: A connector can open a PQRS item when it answers S1 itself.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Electric scooters are being sold in record numbers in Indian cities. **P:** Buyers like them because they cost very little to run. **Q:** Yet charging points are still hard to find outside big cities. **R:** A full charge costs less than a cup of tea. **S:** Until this changes, many families will hesitate to switch. **6.** Oil companies have now promised a charger at every petrol pump.
practice.solution: **P** gives the reason for buying and **R** is its proof (the cheap charge), so they form a pair. 'Yet' in **Q** contrasts with the whole positive case, so it follows **R** rather than S1. **S**'s 'this' is the shortage of charging points, so **Q****S** is a pair. **PRQS**.
practice.shortcut: Here the Yet part answers a part, not S1 — it follows the good news it contradicts.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Food is wasted at almost every Indian wedding. **P:** Meanwhile, thousands in the same city go to bed hungry. **Q:** Much of the leftover food ends up in the garbage. **R:** Hosts often cook for far more guests than actually attend. **S:** Clearly, the extra food must reach those who need it. **6.** Several groups now collect wedding leftovers for night shelters.
practice.solution: **S** begins with 'Clearly' and concludes from everything before it, so it is last. **Q**'s 'the leftover food' needs the extra cooking in **R**. **P**'s 'Meanwhile' contrasts hunger with the waste already described. **RQPS**.
practice.shortcut: 'Clearly' marks the closing part; cause -> waste -> contrast before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Several of India's glaciers are shrinking fast. **P:** Hence, experts say, cutting emissions is now a matter of survival. **Q:** This loss threatens the rivers that millions depend on for water. **R:** As a result, some glaciers have retreated by over a kilometre. **S:** Rising temperatures melt more ice each summer than winter snow can replace. **6.** Saving the glaciers will need action from every country.
practice.solution: 'Hence' marks **P** as the closer. Before it: the cause **S**, 'As a result' **R**, and 'This loss' **Q**, which sums up the retreat. **SRQP**.
practice.shortcut: Closing signal (Hence) last; cause -> result -> 'This loss' before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** India celebrates the harvest in many different ways. **P:** In Punjab, for example, farmers dance the bhangra at Baisakhi. **Q:** In Tamil Nadu, on the other hand, families cook sweet pongal in new pots. **R:** Yet all these festivals share the same spirit of thanksgiving. **S:** Each region has its own harvest festival and its own name for it. **6.** They thank nature for a good crop and pray for the next one.
practice.solution: **S** is the general claim, so it opens. **P**'s 'for example' illustrates it. **Q**'s 'on the other hand' needs a first example before it. **R**'s 'all these festivals' sums up both examples. **SPQR**.
practice.shortcut: General first; 'for example' before 'on the other hand'; 'all these' last.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Sleep is not simply a time when the brain switches off. **P:** A good night's sleep is therefore as important for learning as study itself. **Q:** Scientists have found that it stays busy through the night. **R:** During deep sleep, for instance, it stores the day's memories. **S:** During dream sleep, it sorts and links these memories with older ones. **6.** Students who stay up all night before an exam forget this.
practice.solution: **Q** is the general finding; **R** ('for instance') gives the first specific case, and **S**'s 'these memories' needs **R**. **P**'s 'therefore' concludes, and S6's 'this' refers back to it. **QRSP**.
practice.shortcut: General finding -> 'for instance' -> 'these memories' -> therefore.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A new girl, Meena, joined our class in July. **P:** She had come from a village school that had just twenty students. **Q:** The two soon became inseparable friends. **R:** Our class teacher then asked Anu, the monitor, to help her settle in. **S:** Such a large class made her so nervous that she hardly spoke. **6.** Today Meena is one of the most popular students in school.
practice.solution: 'She' in **P** = Meena from S1. **S**'s 'Such a large class' contrasts with the twenty students in **P**, so the two form a pair. **R**'s 'then' is the teacher's response to her nervousness. **Q**'s 'The two' needs both Meena and Anu, so it follows **R**. **PSRQ**.
practice.shortcut: 'The two' needs both names; 'Such a large class' needs the twenty students.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Kalpana Chawla was born in Karnal, Haryana, in 1962. **P:** There she earned a doctorate and joined NASA. **Q:** In 1997, she became the first woman of Indian origin to fly into space. **R:** After studying aeronautical engineering in Chandigarh, she moved to the United States. **S:** Her second mission, in 2003, ended in tragedy when the shuttle Columbia broke up on its return. **6.** India still remembers her as a hero.
practice.solution: 'There' in **P** needs the country named in **R**, so they form a pair. Joining NASA comes before flying for it, so **P** is before **Q**. 'Her second mission' needs the first flight of 1997, so **Q** is before **S**. **RPQS**.
practice.shortcut: Place word 'There' pairs with the country; 'second mission' follows the first.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** One evening, an old traveller knocked at the door of a poor farmer. **P:** The next morning, the traveller left a small clay pot on the doorstep. **Q:** Inside the pot, the farmer found a bag of seeds and a note. **R:** The farmer shared his simple meal and gave the stranger a mat by the fire. **S:** He asked for some food and a place to rest for the night. **6.** The note said, 'Kindness, like these seeds, always grows.'
practice.solution: 'He' in **S** is the traveller from S1. **R**'s meal and mat answer **S**'s request. **P**'s 'The next morning' follows the night. **P** introduces 'a small clay pot', and **Q**'s 'Inside the pot' refers back to it, so **P****Q** is an a -> the pair. **SRPQ**.
practice.shortcut: a small clay pot -> the pot: the 'a' part comes first.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Last Sunday, my father brought home a second-hand bicycle. **P:** By evening, the bicycle looked almost new. **Q:** A mechanic nearby replaced the chain for fifty rupees. **R:** It came with a rusty chain and a torn seat. **S:** The seat was harder to fix, so my mother stitched a new cover for it. **6.** My sister took the first ride around the colony.
practice.solution: **R** introduces 'a rusty chain and a torn seat'. **Q**'s 'the chain' and **S**'s 'The seat' refer back to it. **S**'s 'harder' compares with the easy chain repair, so **Q****S** is a pair. **P**'s 'By evening' sums up the day's work. **RQSP**.
practice.shortcut: a chain / a seat -> the chain / the seat; 'harder' compares with the part before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Every monsoon, many Mumbai streets flood within hours. **P:** This problem gets worse when plastic waste blocks them. **Q:** The old drains of the city were built for far less rain. **R:** To tackle this, the city now cleans its main drains every May. **S:** This effort has reduced waterlogging at several spots. **6.** Experts, however, say the drains themselves must be rebuilt.
practice.solution: A chain of 'this' words: **P**'s 'This problem' = the undersized drains of **Q**; **R**'s 'To tackle this' = the blocked drains of **P**; **S**'s 'This effort' = the cleaning in **R**. **QPRS**.
practice.shortcut: this problem -> this -> this effort: each sums up the part before it.

practice.q:
